Mutation fixture (two people born in 1976, one 50 at the end of 2025 and one not), inputs of mutation.eic.mfj_no_child_20000 with both years of birth 1976, the taxpayer answering Yes and the spouse No to 'Were you 50 or older at the end of 2025?'; expected values predicted by hand before running the evaluator. i1040gi p. 97, IRA Deduction Worksheet, '$8,000 if age 50 or older at the end of 2025': the taxpayer is (person.ira_age50 true), the spouse is not (person.ira_age50 false). p560 chapter 3, Catch-up contributions, 'age 50 or over at the end of the calendar year' and the 60-to-63 band 'in a tax year in which they attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63': the taxpayer's SIMPLE catch-up band is 50 or over (person.simple_age age50), the spouse's is under 50 (under50).

Mutation fixture (a person born in 1971 who states being 55 at the end of 2025, and a person born in 1970), inputs of mutation.eic.mfj_no_child_20000 with the taxpayer born in 1971 answering Yes to 'Were you age 55 or older at the end of 2025?' and the spouse born in 1970; expected values predicted by hand before running the evaluator. i8889 p. 4, Line 3, rule 6, 'If, at the end of 2025, you were age 55 or older': for a person born in 1971 the year leaves this open and the stated answer decides (person.age55_at_year_end_if_open_year true). The spouse, born in 1970, is 55 at the end of 2025, within 50 to 59 for the SIMPLE catch-up (p560 chapter 3, 'age 50 or over at the end of the calendar year', the higher band only for those who attain 60 to 63 in the year): person.simple_age age50. i5329 p. 8, Lines 52a and 52b, 'following the year in which you reach age 73': the taxpayer, born in 1971, is 54, so not of that age (person.rmd_age false).

Mutation fixture (the SIMPLE catch-up band of people born in 1962 and 1966, as they state it), inputs of mutation.eic.mfj_no_child_20000 with the taxpayer born in 1962 stating the band 50 or over (64 at the end of 2025) and the spouse born in 1966 stating the band 60 to 63 (60 at the end of 2025); expected values predicted by hand before running the evaluator. p560 chapter 3, Catch-up contributions, the higher limit applies 'in a tax year in which they attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63': a person born in 1962 attains 63 or 64 in 2025 and one born in 1966 attains 59 or 60, so the year leaves the band open and the stated answer decides: taxpayer age50 (64, past the band), spouse age60_63 (person.simple_age).

Mutation fixture (a person born in 1960 whose final return this is, having died in 2025 before reaching 65, and a person born in 1961 not on January 1), inputs of mutation.eic.mfj_no_child_20000 with the taxpayer born in 1960 answering Yes to 'Is this the final return of a person who died in 2025 before reaching age 65?' and the spouse born in 1961 answering No to 'Were you born on January 1?'; both have an SSN; expected values predicted by hand before running the evaluator. i1040gi p. 110, Schedule 1-A, Part V, Death of a taxpayer in 2025, 'If a taxpayer was born before January 2, 1961, but died in 2025 before reaching age 65 ...': the taxpayer is such a person (person.died_before_65 true); the taxpayer has an SSN (person.tin_or_itin_applied true; i1040gi p. 17). Mutation fixture (the possibility of a required minimum distribution: by age, and by an inherited account), inputs of mutation.eic.mfj_no_child_20000 with the taxpayer born in 1950 (not asked about an inherited account) and the spouse, born in 1980, answering Yes to the inherited IRA or plan account question; neither missed a required distribution; expected values predicted by hand before running the evaluator. i5329 p. 8, Lines 52a and 52b, a required minimum distribution is due for the year 'following the year in which you reach age 73', and a beneficiary of an inherited account can owe one at any age: the taxpayer (75 at the end of 2025) can owe one (person.rmd_possible true); the spouse inherited an account (person.inherited_account_if_under_73 true), so can owe one (person.rmd_possible true).

The person listed a Form 8889 (person.has_hsa true), and so is asked the earlier-year excess question, answered Yes (person.x_hsa_prior_excess_if_hsa true; i5329 Part VII, Additional Tax on Excess Contributions to Health Savings Accounts, which this tool does not prepare). Born in 1950, the person is of the age at which a required distribution is due (i5329 p. 8, Lines 52a and 52b, 'following the year in which you reach age 73'), so the inherited-account question is not asked and its gate is No (person.inherited_account_if_under_73 false).

cases.evidence_note: Mutation fixture (the Social Security Benefits Worksheet exception for a traditional IRA contribution while covered by a plan), inputs of stage10.refuse.pub915 with its defaults stated, the repayment item answered No, and Yes to 'Did you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) put money into a traditional IRA for 2025 while covered by a retirement plan at work or through self-employment?', with the IRA facts that say so (an IRA, a $3,000 traditional contribution, covered by a plan at work); expected value predicted by hand from the archived i1040gi before running the evaluator: p. 31, Lines 6a and 6b, Exception, the worksheet in the instructions does not apply to a person who made traditional IRA contributions and was covered by a retirement plan; use Pub. 915 or 590-A: line 6b is refused (gate ssb.pub915).

cases.evidence_note: Mutation fixture (whether money went back into a retirement account, for a direct rollover), inputs of stage10.plan.direct_rollover with its defaults stated (a plan distribution of $20,000, code G); expected value predicted by hand from the archived f1099r before running the evaluator: code G is a direct rollover to another plan or IRA (f1099r Box 7, code G), so the money went into another retirement account (person.retirement.put_back true), without the rollover question being asked.

Mutation fixture (code 7 for a person under 59 1/2), inputs of stage10.ira.fully_taxable with its defaults stated, the distribution code 7, Yes to 'Were you under age 59½ when you received any of this money?' and No to 'Is it from a section 457 plan ...?'; expected values predicted by hand from the archived f1099r and i5329 before running the evaluator: code 7 is a normal distribution, for a person 59 1/2 or older (f1099r Box 7, code 7); for a person under 59 1/2 it fits only a section 457 plan distribution not from a rollover, so the code does not fit (person.retirement.code7_wrong true) and the Form 1099-R is refused as needing Form 5329 rules this tool does not apply (person.retirement.screen_refused true).

Mutation fixture (two refusals of one Form 1099-R: the first in order is told), inputs of stage10.refuse.roth_not_q with its defaults stated (a Roth IRA distribution), the distribution code 7, Yes to 'Were you under age 59½ when you received any of this money?' and No to the section 457 question; expected values predicted by hand from the archived i1040gi before running the evaluator: a Roth IRA distribution other than a qualified distribution (code Q) needs Form 8606 (i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2), refused, and that refusal, the first of line 4a's, is the one line 4a carries (f1040.line4a, gate bad_code); the code 7 for a person under 59 1/2 also does not fit (person.retirement.screen_refused true), a later refusal.

f1040.line4a.remedy: A Roth IRA distribution other than a qualified distribution (code Q), code S other than from a traditional SIMPLE IRA, code 3 other than from an IRA, or a distribution code other than 7, 4, 2, 1, S, 3, G or Q, is outside this tool.

cases.evidence_note: Mutation fixture (an amount in box 5 of an IRA distribution's Form 1099-R does not make it partly nontaxable), inputs of stage10.ira.fully_taxable with its defaults stated (a traditional IRA distribution of $10,000, code 7) and $500 entered in box 5; expected values predicted by hand from the archived i1040gi before running the evaluator: box 5 is for after-tax employee contributions and premiums under plans and annuities (i1099r, Box 5), not for IRAs, whose nontaxable part comes from Form 8606; with no rollover, no Roth account and no basis the IRA distribution is fully taxable, so line 4a is left blank (person.retirement.amount_a $0) and the whole $10,000 goes on line 4b (i1040gi p. 26, Lines 4a and 4b).

Mutation fixture (T-250: the taxpayers operand of household.roster_ok, read as persons by the mutant), predicted from spec 4.7 before evaluating: the inputs of ss.person.separation (fixtures/2025/s3.json) with its defaults applied, a single filer with two person entries, taxpayer (role taxpayer) and second, whose role is unanswered (no default is stated for it). household.taxpayers counts the entries whose role is taxpayer: the taxpayer's entry counts 1 and the second entry's where-test is unknown, so the count is unknown with lower bound 1 (spec 4.7.5; person.role has no refusal gate, so it is not gate-pending), and 'taxpayers = 1' is not decided by the bound (it decides eq false only above 1), so it is unknown; household.spouses is unknown the same way (lower bound 0). Gates of roster_ok: no birth year is bad and nobody is under 16, both counts a known 0. roster_ok's first conjunction is false (status single, not mfj); its second is all[status not mfj (true), taxpayers = 1 (unknown), spouses = 0 (unknown)], unknown; so roster_ok and roster_bad (roster_ok = false) are unknown, carrying the first unknown met, the taxpayers count's (the second entry's role, lower bound 1: a comparison and the tests above it pass an unknown operand on unchanged, spec 4.7.2; the first run of the case showed that bound, which this prediction had left out). With persons (every entry, 2) in place of taxpayers, 'persons = 1' is false, roster_ok is false and roster_bad is true, so this case kills the mutant.
